dek: The ARChitects’ grid solver earned Franzen two Kaggle golds. His prize-winning version of Duck gave rival teams a way into ARC-AGI-3.
headline: Daniel “the Duck” Franzen makes the field play his game

image.alt: Daniel Franzen wears two overlapping gold medals, a cyan grid eyepiece and a three-fan graphics card while working on a wheeled robot that operates an arcade joystick.
image.caption: Daniel Franzen’s two Kaggle golds came from a win and a runner-up finish with the ARChitects.

sections.text: Daniel Franzen gave his version of the Duck agent an undo button. He let it see what moved between frames and which squares changed after a move. When the rules are hidden, a wrong move can still teach you something. Other ARC-AGI-3 entrants took that notebook into the contest. Now his name is on the Generalist Gaming board, and anyone scouting him has a notebook to read.

sections.heading: Turn the board around
sections.text:
At Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz, Franzen and Michael Wand wrote a NeurIPS paper on networks that keep track of what happens when an image turns. Away from the lab, Franzen grows Riesling in the Moselle valley.

The ARChitects made different views of the same grid work for them. Their solver generated possible answers and used the same model to score them. They won the ARC Prize 2024 high-score contest. Franzen, Jan Disselhoff and David Hartmann published the method at ICML and returned to the podium the following year with a solver that could revise its grid guesses. The runner-up finish earned Franzen another Kaggle gold.

sections.heading: How the Duck got around
sections.text:
Jeroen Cottaar and Tufa Labs built the original Duck harness, which lets an agent inspect a game and make moves. Franzen adapted it to give promising games more time and to show the agent more of what happened after a move. He released the notebook and won the open-source prize for ARC-AGI-3’s second milestone.

Then came the forks. Pathbreaker adapted Franzen’s agent for a selected final submission. Keeper built on his release and tested the agent’s guesses about the rules against the moves it had played. Team Turducken credits the same notebook as its starting point. Mark Barney, editor of The Loose Goose, is a member of Team Turducken.

sections.heading: Where the ARChitects landed
sections.text:
The ARChitects’ ARC-AGI-3 lineup was Franzen, Disselhoff, Hartmann and Sebastian Brodehl. The team stood #14 at 47.19 on Kaggle’s closed public board. ARC Prize is scheduled to announce the competition results on December 4.

Generalist Gaming is the next test. Can Franzen turn the same knack for reading unfamiliar rules into another run at the top?
